families.basis: Family centers follow the sRGB primaries/secondaries and the measured colour-term patches of Jonauskaite, Parraga, Quiblier & Mohr (2020), Table 1, converted xyY -> OKLCH. Boundaries sit between those anchors; they are a convention, not a finding.

neutral.note: Any hue with OKLCH C below 0.03 counts as neutral.

colorTerms.tier: anchors: measured (single study's chosen prototypes); bands: low confidence (engineering choice)
colorTerms.note: Bridges the literature's colour WORDS to regions. Anchor = the study's patch (Munsell + xyY, Table 1) in OKLCH. The study's 'purple' patch (7.5P 4/10) lands at h 324, inside magenta; its purple term/patch agreement was only .23, so purple is split across both families.

royal blue.note: Separate blue for the Labrecque & Milne (2012) words (competent, reliable, intelligent, successful), added 2026-10-06 (C14 decision 3, C9 option 3). Study 1 gives saturation 220/240 and lightness 120/240 in HSL but no hue angle; hue 240 is assumed, the RGB primary Study 2 states it used. The blue in the printed Fig. 1 (sampled, so approximate) agrees on lightness (OKLCH L 0.43) and hue (269 against 265) and is less saturated (C 0.15 against 0.30, which is expected from print). The anchor is used only to break ties between equal scores, so a loud blue wins ties for these words. The band edges are the same as the shared blue region and are still an engineering choice. The shared blue region keeps the Jonauskaite et al. sky blue (hue 233) for the Jonauskaite-based words.

ou2004.cite: Ou, Luo, Woodcock & Wright (2004). A study of colour emotion and colour preference. Part I: Colour emotions for single colours. Color Research & Application 29(3), 232-240.
ou2004.scope: 31 observers (14 British, 17 Chinese), 20 NCS patches on mid-grey under D65. Models in CIELAB: WC R2 .74, HL R2 .76, AP R2 .75, HS R2 .73. Equations checked against the printed paper, Eqs. 2-5 p. 238, 2026-10-04 (TO-CONFIRM X11). The paper has no models for its other six scales (C17, closed). Observers were all members of a color-science institute with color-science training (17 staff, 8 PhD students, 6 MSc students), not a general sample. Patches were 3 x 3 inch, viewed one at a time in a dark room; judgments were forced-choice word pairs scored as Thurstone Case V z-scores, so WC > 0 means most observers chose warm. The authors call the four modeled scales culture-independent across Britain, China, Japan, Thailand and Hong Kong only; tense-relaxed and like-dislike differed between British and Chinese observers and are not modeled. The paper does not state the white point of its CIELAB values (the engine's D65 frame is inferred from the D65 viewing cabinet). Limits recorded 2026-10-13.

cie_ilv.cite: CIE S 017:2020 International Lighting Vocabulary, terms 17-22-063 (lightness) and 17-22-074 (chroma).
cie_ilv.scope: Definitions of the perceptual attributes; no thresholds.

lm2012.cite: Labrecque & Milne (2012). Exciting red and competent blue: the importance of color in marketing. Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 40, 711-727.
lm2012.scope: Study 1: n=255, fictitious logos, 10 colours vs grey (HSL S 220/240, L 120/240). Study 2: n=291, red/green/blue/purple x saturation (100%/42%) x value (100%/58%). US samples. Coefficients first read from an academia.edu copy by automated extraction; the kept values were checked against the printed Tables 1-2 on 2026-10-06 and match (TO-CONFIRM C14).

aaker1997.cite: Aaker (1997). Dimensions of Brand Personality. Journal of Marketing Research 34(3), 347-356.
aaker1997.scope: Five dimensions, 15 facets. Facet names checked against secondary summaries; the article itself is paywalled.

jon2024.cite: Jonauskaite et al. (2024). A comparative analysis of colour-emotion associations in 16-88-year-old adults from 31 countries. British Journal of Psychology 115, 275-305.
jon2024.scope: n=7,393, 31 countries, 12 colour TERMS x 20 emotions (Geneva Emotion Wheel). Reports the 14 associations chosen by at least 40% of participants.

jon2020ps.cite: Jonauskaite et al. (2020). Universal patterns in color-emotion associations are further shaped by linguistic and geographic proximity. Psychological Science 31(10).
jon2020ps.scope: n=4,598, 30 nations; average pattern similarity r = .88. Supports universality, not specific shades.

jon2020ip.cite: Jonauskaite, Parraga, Quiblier & Mohr (2020). Feeling blue or seeing red? Similar patterns of emotion associations with colour patches and colour terms. i-Perception 11(1).
jon2020ip.scope: n=132, Switzerland. Patch vs term pattern r = .82 (purple .23). Table 1 gives Munsell + xyY for the 12 patches.

jon2024_data.cite: Jonauskaite et al. (2024), raw data (DATA.csv) from the OSF project for the BJP article; 7,387 unique participants, 88,716 participant x colour records.
jon2024_data.scope: Reproduces all 14 published >= 40% figures exactly. Weights derived by build/emotion_weights.py: rate >= 1.25 x the emotion's mean across colours AND in the emotion's top 3 in >= 50% of the 25 countries with >= 100 participants.

vikalpa2008.cite: Measurement and Validity of Jennifer Aaker's Brand Personality Scale for Colgate Brand (2008). Vikalpa 33(3). Reproduces Aaker's (1997) 42 trait items by dimension.
vikalpa2008.scope: Secondary source for the wording of Aaker's 42 items (listed by dimension only, p. 52). The grouping of items into facets is not in this source; it was checked against Aaker (1997) Appendix A (TO-CONFIRM C16, closed 2026-10-03).

rows.rule: Ou warm-cool WC > 0: reds through yellows with enough chroma
rows.notes: WC = -0.5 + 0.02 C*^1.07 cos(h - 50deg). About 32% of an sRGB grid scores warm.

rows.rule: Ou WC < 0, leaning toward cyan and blue; neutral greys allowed (D40)
rows.notes: WC alone scores every near-neutral as cool (WC = -0.5 at C* 0). In phase 3 a hue lean was added from the model's own cos(h - 50deg) term at each family's centre (converted to CIELAB D65 hue) so that greys would rank below blues and cyans. D40 (Kwade, 2026-10-13, after reading Gao & Xin 2006, Gao et al. 2007, Xin et al. 2004 and Ou et al. 2004, all of which rate grayish and low-chroma colours cool) lets greys rank as cool again: the neutral family now has a hue weight of 0.38, so a true grey is offered as a seed after cyan and blue. 0.38 is 0.80 x (0.50 / 1.05): Ou's mean cool score (-WC) over the matcher's sRGB grid for the neutral family, 0.50, against blue, 1.05, with the blue weight of 0.80 kept. It is an engineering choice (low confidence). D42 (Kwade, 2026-10-13, TO-CONFIRM C34) raises purple from 0.25 to 0.55 and green from 0.13 to 0.35, the same calculation scaled so that blue stays 0.80. Two grids gave purple 0.54 to 0.62 and green 0.35 to 0.42; the lower values, from a second check on the same day, were used (purple 0.81 to 0.84 and green 0.52 to 0.53 against blue 1.19 to 1.24 on Ou's scale). The cyan, blue and neutral weights were not re-derived: the two grids disagreed on cyan and blue by up to 0.2. Low confidence. A family weight is an average: inside a family the score varies with hue (a yellow-green is only weakly cool on Ou's scale), which one number cannot show.
rows.kwadeNote: Approved 2026-09-28; hue lean added from Ou's WC term; greys allowed with neutral weight 0.38 (D40, 2026-10-13); purple 0.55 and green 0.35 (D42, 2026-10-13)

rows.rule: Ou heavy-light HL > 0: CIELAB L* below 58 (about OKLCH L 0.64)
rows.notes: HL = -2.1 + 0.05(100 - L*); depends on lightness only.

rows.rule: Ou HL < 0: CIELAB L* above 58 (about OKLCH L 0.64)
rows.notes: Ou's pole is 'light'; renamed 'airy' so it doesn't collide with the lightness term 'light'. Same direction.

rows.rule: Ou active-passive AP > 0.5: far from mid-grey in chroma or lightness
rows.notes: AP > 0 covers ~81% of an sRGB grid, so the 0.5 floor is an engineering choice to make the term selective.

rows.rule: Ou AP < 0: close to mid-grey, low chroma
rows.notes: Ou's word is 'passive'; using it for 'calm' is a lexical choice for Kwade to confirm.

rows.rule: Ou hard-soft HS > 0: darker and lower-chroma colours
rows.notes: HS = 11.1 + 0.03(100 - L*) - 11.4 C*^0.02. Exact neutrals (C* 0) score very hard, an artifact of the C*^0.02 term.

rows.notes: Strongest soft scores in sRGB are light yellows.
